# Statistical Inference **Week 5**: Comparing groups with t-tests, one-way ANOVA and two-way ANOVA In this workshop you will learn the three most common tests for comparing **groups**: the two-sample *t*-test, the one-way ANOVA and the two-way ANOVA. They might look like three different tests, but they are all the same idea, a **linear model with categorical predictors**, so learning one makes the next one easy. Workshop materials are available in the GitHub repository [ECS200](https://github.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop). ![](images/base_model.png) ::: {.callout-tip} ## Learning outcomes By the end of this workshop you should be able to: 1. Choose between a *t*-test, one-way ANOVA and two-way ANOVA for a research question. 2. Visualise group data and check the assumptions of these tests. 3. Run each test in R and find the important numbers in the output. 4. Write a results sentence that reports the direction, size and statistical support of an effect. ::: ## Before we start {.unnumbered} Download this week's data and save it in the `data` folder of your workshop folder (see [Introduction to R](R_intro.qmd) for how the folder is set up). [ lizard_sprint.csv](data/lizard_sprint.csv){.btn .btn-outline-danger .btn-sm .download-btn download="lizard_sprint.csv"} Create a new R script with the usual header and load the packages. We will use one new package this week, `performance`, which draws all the assumption-checking plots for a model in one line (the plots themselves come from its partner package, `see`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Week 5 workshop - Statistical inference # Written by Nicholas Wu, 1234578, 25/03/2027 # Install new packages (only needed once, run in the console) # install.packages("performance") # install.packages("see") # Load packages library(tidyverse) # data import, wrangling and plotting library(performance) # checking model assumptions library(see) # draws the plots for the performance package # Set your working directory to your workshop folder # setwd("C:/Users/YOUR-NAME/Documents/ECS200") ``` ::: ### Study context {.unnumbered} Lizards are ectotherms, so their body temperature, and therefore how fast they can run, depends on the temperature around them. Performance usually increases with temperature up to an optimum and then drops off quickly (a *thermal performance curve*). Populations from hotter places often have a higher optimum. To test this, 72 adult dragons were collected from a **coastal** (mild) and an **inland** (hot) population. In the lab, each lizard was randomly assigned to one test temperature (**20, 28 or 36 °C**), warmed to that temperature, and raced once along a 1 m racetrack to measure its maximum **sprint speed** (m/s). Each lizard was used only once, so every row is an independent lizard. ![A mountain heath dragon (*Rankinia diemensis*).](images/Rankinia_diemensis.jpg){width=70%} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load the data lizard_data <- readr::read_csv("data/lizard_sprint.csv") # Check the structure: temperature is stored as a number, but in this # experiment it is a treatment group, so we convert it to a factor. lizard_data <- lizard_data %>% dplyr::mutate(temperature = factor(temperature, levels = c(20, 28, 36)), population = factor(population)) dplyr::glimpse(lizard_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 72 Columns: 5 $ lizard_id "L01", "L02", "L03", "L04", "L05", "L06", "L07", "L08", "… $ population inland, coastal, coastal, coastal, inland, coastal, coast… $ temperature 36, 28, 28, 28, 28, 36, 20, 20, 20, 20, 36, 28, 36, 36, 2… $ mass_g 13.5, 16.1, 10.1, 10.1, 12.3, 10.9, 12.5, 12.4, 12.4, 14.… $ sprint_speed 1.60, 1.53, 1.81, 1.92, 1.44, 1.92, 0.95, 1.49, 1.09, 1.2… ``` ::: ::: ### Which test do I use? {.unnumbered} All three tests ask the same question: *is the difference between group means bigger than we would expect from random variation alone?* They differ only in how many groups and how many predictors you have. | Research question | Predictor(s) | Test | R function | |:------------------|:-------------|:-----|:-----------| | Do **two** groups differ? | 1 categorical variable with 2 levels | Two-sample *t*-test | `t.test()` | | Do **three or more** groups differ? | 1 categorical variable with 3+ levels | One-way ANOVA | `aov()` | | Do **two** factors affect the response, and does the effect of one depend on the other? | 2 categorical variables | Two-way ANOVA | `aov(y ~ A * B)` | ::: {.callout-note} Functions without a package name in front, such as `t.test()`, `aov()` and `lm()`, come with R itself (the `stats` package), so you never need to install or load them. ::: # Part A: Two groups (*t*-test) {.unnumbered} **Question**: Do lizards sprint faster at 28 °C than at 20 °C? ## 1. Background {.unnumbered} A two-sample *t*-test compares the **means of two independent groups**. It calculates a *t* value: $$ t = \frac{\text{difference between the two group means}}{\text{standard error of that difference}} = \frac{\text{signal}}{\text{noise}} $$ A large *t* (a big difference relative to the variation within groups) gives a small *p*-value. Three things make a difference easier to detect: - a **bigger difference** between the means (more signal); - **less variation** within each group (less noise); - a **larger sample size** (the standard error shrinks as *n* grows). R uses **Welch's *t*-test** by default. It does not assume the two groups have equal variances, so it is a safe default for ecological data. Use the app below to see how these three ingredients change the result. Every time you move a slider, a new experiment is simulated in your browser. ::: {.app-box .column-body-outset} ::: {.app-title} App: signal versus noise in a *t*-test ::: ::: {.app-grid} ::: {.app-controls} ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| output: false import {rng, rnorm, mean, sd, welch, qt975, fmt, fmtp, red, grey, dark} from "./apps/ecs200.js" ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof tt_diff = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "True difference between means (m/s)"}) viewof tt_sd = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.8], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Variation within groups (SD)"}) viewof tt_n = Inputs.range([3, 50], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Lizards per group (n)"}) viewof tt_seed = Inputs.button("Resample") ``` ::: ::: {.app-output} ```{ojs} //| echo: false tt_data = { const r = rng(101 + tt_seed); const a = rnorm(r, tt_n, 1.2, tt_sd); const b = rnorm(r, tt_n, 1.2 + tt_diff, tt_sd); const pts = [ ...a.map((v) => ({group: "20 °C", x: 1 + (r() - 0.5) * 0.25, y: v})), ...b.map((v) => ({group: "28 °C", x: 2 + (r() - 0.5) * 0.25, y: v})) ]; const summ = [[a, 1], [b, 2]].map(([g, x]) => { const m = mean(g), half = qt975(g.length - 1) * sd(g) / Math.sqrt(g.length); return {x: x + 0.3, m, lo: m - half, hi: m + half}; }); return {a, b, pts, summ, test: welch(a, b)}; } Plot.plot({ width: 560, height: 300, marginLeft: 50, x: {domain: [0.5, 2.7], ticks: [1, 2], tickFormat: (d) => (d === 1 ? "20 °C" : "28 °C"), label: null}, y: {label: "Sprint speed (m/s)", grid: true}, marks: [ Plot.dot(tt_data.pts, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: grey, fillOpacity: 0.6, r: 3.5}), Plot.ruleX(tt_data.summ, {x: "x", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", stroke: red, strokeWidth: 2.5}), Plot.dot(tt_data.summ, {x: "x", y: "m", fill: red, r: 6}) ] }) html`
Welch's t = ${fmt(tt_data.test.t)}, df = ${fmt(tt_data.test.df, 1)}, p ${fmtp(tt_data.test.p)}. ${tt_data.test.p < 0.05 ? "The difference is statistically significant: it is large compared with the noise." : "The difference is not statistically significant: we cannot separate it from random noise with this sample."} Red points and bars show each group's mean and 95% confidence interval.
` ``` ::: ::: ::: **Try this**: set the true difference to 0 and press *Resample* many times. About 1 in 20 experiments will still be "significant" just by chance. That is what a significance level of α = 0.05 means. **Hypotheses**: - Null hypothesis (H~0~): mean sprint speed is the same at 20 °C and 28 °C. - Alternative hypothesis (H~1~): mean sprint speed differs between 20 °C and 28 °C. - Significance level: α = 0.05. ## 2. Visualise {.unnumbered} First keep only the two temperatures we want to compare, then plot the raw data. A boxplot with the raw points on top shows the centre, spread, shape and any extreme values of each group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Keep only the 20 and 28 degree lizards for the t-test lizard_two <- lizard_data %>% dplyr::filter(temperature %in% c("20", "28")) %>% dplyr::mutate(temperature = droplevels(temperature)) # drop the unused 36 level # Boxplot with the raw data ggplot2::ggplot(lizard_two, ggplot2::aes(x = temperature, y = sprint_speed)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey90") + # hide boxplot outliers (raw points show them) ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.6) + # raw data, spread sideways ggplot2::labs(x = "Test temperature (°C)", y = "Sprint speed (m/s)") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week05_inference_files/figure-html/ttest-vis-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Descriptive statistics for each group lizard_two %>% dplyr::group_by(temperature) %>% dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(sprint_speed), sd = sd(sprint_speed), n = dplyr::n()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 temperature mean sd n 1 20 1.21 0.226 24 2 28 1.82 0.273 24 ``` ::: ::: Lizards at 28 °C look faster than lizards at 20 °C, both groups have a similar spread and there are no extreme values. ## 3. Check assumptions {.unnumbered} | Assumption | How to check | Here | |:-----------|:-------------|:-----| | **Independence**: each observation is from a different, unrelated unit | Think about the study design | ✅ Each lizard was raced once at one temperature. | | **Normality**: the data in each group are roughly bell-shaped | Histogram or Q-Q plot for each group | ✅ See below. | | **Equal variances** (only for the classic *t*-test) | Compare the SDs. If the largest SD is less than 2 × the smallest, they are similar enough | ✅ Similar SDs, and Welch's test does not need this anyway. | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Q-Q plot for each group: points should fall close to the line ggplot2::ggplot(lizard_two, ggplot2::aes(sample = sprint_speed)) + ggplot2::stat_qq() + ggplot2::stat_qq_line() + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ temperature) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sprint speed (m/s)") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week05_inference_files/figure-html/ttest-qq-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"} ## When is a *t*-test NOT appropriate? (click to expand) | What you see | Why it is a problem | What to do instead | |:-------------|:--------------------|:-------------------| | Strongly skewed data or big outliers, especially with small samples | The mean is pulled around by extreme values | Log-transform the response (Week 2), or use the non-parametric **Wilcoxon rank-sum test**, `wilcox.test(y ~ group, data = ...)` | | The same individuals measured twice (before/after, left/right) | Observations are not independent | **Paired *t*-test**, `t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)`, or a mixed model (Week 12) | | The response is a count (e.g. number of seedlings) with many zeros | Counts are not normally distributed | Generalised linear model for counts (Week 8) | | The response is yes/no (e.g. alive/dead) | Not a continuous measurement | Logistic regression (Week 11) | | More than two groups | Running many *t*-tests inflates false positives | One-way ANOVA (Part B) | For example, the Wilcoxon test compares the *ranks* of the values instead of the values themselves, so a single extreme value has little influence: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wilcox.test(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_two) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Wilcoxon rank sum exact test data: sprint_speed by temperature W = 25.5, p-value = 6.085e-10 alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## 4. Model {.unnumbered} The formula `response ~ group` reads "sprint speed *explained by* temperature". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Welch two-sample t-test (two-sided) lizard_ttest <- t.test(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_two) lizard_ttest ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: sprint_speed by temperature t = -8.3763, df = 44.412, p-value = 1.088e-10 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 20 and group 28 is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -0.7515599 -0.4601067 sample estimates: mean in group 20 mean in group 28 1.212083 1.817917 ``` ::: ::: ## 5. Interpret {.unnumbered} ![](images/base_communicate.png) The output gives everything you need: - `t = ...`: the *t* value. Its sign only tells you which group was first alphabetically. - `df = ...`: degrees of freedom (Welch's test gives a decimal value). - `p-value = ...`: the probability of seeing a difference this large if the null hypothesis were true. - `95 percent confidence interval`: the likely range for the true difference in means (group 1 minus group 2). If it does not include 0, the difference is significant at α = 0.05. - `sample estimates`: the mean of each group. **Methods sentence**: *Sprint speed of lizards tested at 20 °C and 28 °C was compared using a two-sided Welch's two-sample* t*-test in R (version 4.5.1). Significance was set with α = 0.05.* ::: {.cell} ::: **Results sentence** (direction + size + statistical support + figure): > Lizards sprinted faster at 28 °C (mean ± SD = 1.82 ± 0.27 m/s) > than at 20 °C (1.21 ± 0.23 m/s), an average increase of > 0.61 m/s (95% CI 0.46 to 0.75 m/s; > Welch's *t*~44.4~ = 8.38, *p* < 0.001; Fig. 1). # Part B: Three or more groups (one-way ANOVA) {.unnumbered} **Question**: Does sprint speed differ among the three test temperatures (20, 28 and 36 °C)? ## 1. Background {.unnumbered} With three groups you could run three *t*-tests (20 vs 28, 20 vs 36, 28 vs 36), but every extra test adds another 5% chance of a false positive. A **one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA)** asks a single question first: *do all groups share the same mean, or does at least one differ?* ANOVA compares two kinds of variation: - **Between-group** variation: how far the group means are from the overall mean (signal). - **Within-group** variation: how spread out individuals are inside each group (noise). $$ F = \frac{\text{variation between groups}}{\text{variation within groups}} $$ A large *F* means the group means are further apart than the noise would suggest. If the ANOVA is significant, a **post hoc test** (Tukey's HSD) then tells you *which* groups differ, while keeping the overall false-positive rate at 5%. ::: {.app-box .column-body-outset} ::: {.app-title} App: between- versus within-group variation ::: ::: {.app-grid} ::: {.app-controls} ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| output: false import {anova1} from "./apps/ecs200.js" ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof an_spread = Inputs.range([0, 0.6], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Spread of the group means (signal)"}) viewof an_sd = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.8], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Variation within groups (noise)"}) viewof an_n = Inputs.range([3, 30], {value: 12, step: 1, label: "Lizards per group (n)"}) viewof an_seed = Inputs.button("Resample") ``` ::: ::: {.app-output} ```{ojs} //| echo: false an_data = { const r = rng(202 + an_seed); const mus = [1.6 - an_spread, 1.6 + an_spread, 1.6]; const labels = ["20 °C", "28 °C", "36 °C"]; const groups = mus.map((m) => rnorm(r, an_n, m, an_sd)); const pts = groups.flatMap((g, i) => g.map((v) => ({x: i + 1 + (r() - 0.5) * 0.3, y: v, group: labels[i]}))); const means = groups.map((g, i) => ({x1: i + 0.7, x2: i + 1.3, m: mean(g)})); return {pts, means, grand: mean(groups.flat()), res: anova1(groups)}; } Plot.plot({ width: 560, height: 350, marginLeft: 50, x: {domain: [0.5, 3.5], ticks: [1, 2, 3], tickFormat: (d) => ["20 °C", "28 °C", "36 °C"][d - 1], label: null}, y: {label: "Sprint speed (m/s)", grid: true}, marks: [ Plot.ruleY([an_data.grand], {stroke: dark, strokeDasharray: "5,4"}), Plot.dot(an_data.pts, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: grey, fillOpacity: 0.6, r: 3}), Plot.link(an_data.means, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: "m", y2: "m", stroke: red, strokeWidth: 4}) ] }) html`
One-way ANOVA: F${an_data.res.df1},${an_data.res.df2} = ${fmt(an_data.res.F)}, p ${fmtp(an_data.res.p)}. Red lines are the group means and the dashed line is the overall (grand) mean. ${an_data.res.p < 0.05 ? "At least one group mean differs." : "No evidence that the group means differ."}
` ``` ::: ::: ::: **Hypotheses**: - H~0~: mean sprint speed is the same at all three temperatures. - H~1~: at least one temperature has a different mean sprint speed. ## 2. Visualise {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Boxplot with raw data for all three temperatures ggplot2::ggplot(lizard_data, ggplot2::aes(x = temperature, y = sprint_speed)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey90") + ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.6) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Test temperature (°C)", y = "Sprint speed (m/s)") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week05_inference_files/figure-html/anova-vis-1.png){width=528} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Mean, SD and sample size per temperature lizard_data %>% dplyr::group_by(temperature) %>% dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(sprint_speed), sd = sd(sprint_speed), n = dplyr::n()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 temperature mean sd n 1 20 1.21 0.226 24 2 28 1.82 0.273 24 3 36 1.80 0.249 24 ``` ::: ::: Speed looks lowest at 20 °C and highest at 28 °C, and the spread is similar across groups. ## 3. Check assumptions {.unnumbered} The assumptions are the same as for the *t*-test (independence, normality and equal variances), but for ANOVA we check them on the **residuals**. A residual is the distance between an observation and its group mean, the part of the data the model cannot explain. The `performance::check_model()` function draws the main diagnostic plots, and each panel has a subtitle telling you what a "good" plot looks like. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fit the one-way ANOVA first, then check its residuals lizard_aov <- aov(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_data) performance::check_model(lizard_aov, check = c("homogeneity", "qq")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week05_inference_files/figure-html/anova-check-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: | Assumption | Plot | Here | |:-----------|:-----|:-----| | **Equal variances** | *Homogeneity of variance*: the reference line should be flat and horizontal | ✅ Roughly flat. | | **Normal residuals** | *Normality of residuals*: dots should fall along the line | ✅ Dots follow the line. | | **Independence** | Study design | ✅ One lizard per measurement. | ::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"} ## When is a one-way ANOVA NOT appropriate? (click to expand) | What you see | What to do instead | |:-------------|:-------------------| | Very unequal spread among groups (largest SD > 2 × smallest) | **Welch's ANOVA**, `oneway.test(y ~ group, data = ...)`, which does not assume equal variances | | Strongly skewed data or outliers with small samples | Log-transform, or the non-parametric **Kruskal–Wallis test**, `kruskal.test(y ~ group, data = ...)` | | Repeated measurements on the same individuals or sites | Mixed-effects model (Week 12) | | Counts or yes/no responses | Generalised linear models (Weeks 8 and 11) | | A numeric predictor (e.g. temperature measured as 18.2, 22.7, 25.1 °C...) | Linear regression (Week 7) | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Example: Kruskal-Wallis test, the non-parametric alternative kruskal.test(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test data: sprint_speed by temperature Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 38.754, df = 2, p-value = 3.843e-09 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## 4. Model {.unnumbered} We already fitted the model above with `aov()`. `summary()` gives the ANOVA table. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ANOVA table summary(lizard_aov) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) temperature 2 5.670 2.8350 45.33 2.69e-13 *** Residuals 69 4.315 0.0625 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Which temperatures differ? Tukey's honestly significant difference test TukeyHSD(lizard_aov) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Tukey multiple comparisons of means 95% family-wise confidence level Fit: aov(formula = sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_data) $temperature diff lwr upr p adj 28-20 0.60583333 0.4329134 0.7787533 0.0000000 36-20 0.58416667 0.4112467 0.7570866 0.0000000 36-28 -0.02166667 -0.1945866 0.1512533 0.9515937 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## ANOVA is a linear model (click to expand) You get exactly the same *F* test with `lm()`. The `lm()` summary also shows the difference of each group from the first (reference) group and the R^2^, the proportion of variation in sprint speed explained by temperature. This is the link to linear regression in Week 7. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lizard_lm <- lm(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_data) summary(lizard_lm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_data) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -0.55625 -0.17771 -0.00208 0.13583 0.60375 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 1.21208 0.05105 23.745 < 2e-16 *** temperature28 0.60583 0.07219 8.392 3.83e-12 *** temperature36 0.58417 0.07219 8.092 1.36e-11 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 0.2501 on 69 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.5678, Adjusted R-squared: 0.5553 F-statistic: 45.33 on 2 and 69 DF, p-value: 2.689e-13 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## 5. Interpret {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ::: Reading the output: - **ANOVA table**: temperature has 2 and 69 degrees of freedom, *F* = 45.33 and *p* < 0.001, so at least one temperature differs. - **Tukey's HSD**: each row is one pair of temperatures. `diff` is the difference in means, `lwr` and `upr` are its 95% confidence interval, and `p adj` is the *p*-value adjusted for making three comparisons. **Methods sentence**: *Differences in sprint speed among three test temperatures (20 °C, 28 °C, 36 °C) were tested with a one-way ANOVA using the `aov()` function, followed by Tukey's HSD post hoc comparisons with the `TukeyHSD()` function in R. Model assumptions were checked with residual diagnostic plots with the `check_model()` from the performance R package [@Ludecke2021].* **Results sentence**: > Sprint speed differed among test temperatures (one-way ANOVA: > *F*~2,69~ = 45.33, *p* < 0.001; > R^2^ = 0.57; Fig. 2). Lizards were 0.61 m/s faster at 28 °C > than at 20 °C (95% CI 0.43–0.78, Tukey *p* < 0.001) and > 0.58 m/s faster at 36 °C than at 20 °C (*p* < 0.001), but speed at 28 °C > and 36 °C did not differ (difference = -0.02 m/s, *p* = 0.95). # Part C: Two factors (two-way ANOVA) {.unnumbered} **Question**: Does the effect of temperature on sprint speed differ between the coastal and inland populations? ## 1. Background {.unnumbered} A **two-way ANOVA** tests two categorical predictors at once (here temperature and population) and, most importantly, their **interaction**. Three questions are tested: 1. **Main effect of temperature**: averaged over both populations, does speed change with temperature? 2. **Main effect of population**: averaged over all temperatures, is one population faster? 3. **Interaction (temperature × population)**: does the effect of temperature *depend on* which population the lizard came from? If there is no interaction, the lines on an **interaction plot** (mean of each group joined by population) are parallel. If the lines are not parallel or they cross, the effect of one factor depends on the other. Use the app to build some interaction plots. ::: {.app-box .column-body-outset} ::: {.app-title} App: what does an interaction look like? ::: ::: {.app-grid} ::: {.app-controls} ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof ix_temp = Inputs.range([-0.4, 0.4], {value: 0.25, step: 0.05, label: "Temperature effect (change per step: 20 → 28 → 36 °C)"}) viewof ix_pop = Inputs.range([-0.4, 0.4], {value: 0.1, step: 0.05, label: "Population effect (inland minus coastal)"}) viewof ix_int = Inputs.range([-0.4, 0.4], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Interaction (extra temperature effect for inland lizards)"}) ``` ::: ::: {.app-output} ```{ojs} //| echo: false ix_means = { const temps = ["20 °C", "28 °C", "36 °C"]; const out = []; temps.forEach((t, i) => { out.push({temp: t, pop: "coastal", mean: 1.4 + ix_temp * i}); out.push({temp: t, pop: "inland", mean: 1.4 + ix_pop + (ix_temp + ix_int) * i}); }); return out; } Plot.plot({ width: 560, height: 300, marginLeft: 50, x: {domain: ["20 °C", "28 °C", "36 °C"], label: "Test temperature", padding: 0.3}, y: {label: "Mean sprint speed (m/s)", grid: true, domain: [0.3, 2.6]}, color: {domain: ["coastal", "inland"], range: [grey, red], legend: true}, marks: [ Plot.line(ix_means, {x: "temp", y: "mean", stroke: "pop", strokeWidth: 3}), Plot.dot(ix_means, {x: "temp", y: "mean", fill: "pop", r: 6}) ] }) html`
${ix_int === 0 ? "Interaction = 0, so the lines are parallel: temperature has the same effect in both populations and you can interpret each main effect on its own." : "Interaction ≠ 0, so the lines are not parallel: the effect of temperature depends on the population. ` ``` ::: ::: ::: ![A visual explanation of interactive effects.](images/interactions_explained.jpg){width=100%} ## 2. Visualise {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Mean and standard error for every temperature x population combination lizard_summary <- lizard_data %>% dplyr::group_by(temperature, population) %>% dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(sprint_speed), se = sd(sprint_speed) / sqrt(dplyr::n()), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") # remove the grouping after summarising lizard_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 5 temperature population mean se n 1 20 coastal 1.2 0.0728 12 2 20 inland 1.22 0.0595 12 3 28 coastal 1.94 0.0720 12 4 28 inland 1.70 0.0718 12 5 36 coastal 1.68 0.0664 12 6 36 inland 1.91 0.0628 12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Interaction plot: raw data (faint) with group means +/- SE joined by lines ggplot2::ggplot() + ggplot2::geom_jitter(data = lizard_data, ggplot2::aes(x = temperature, y = sprint_speed, colour = population), position = ggplot2::position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1, dodge.width = 0.4), alpha = 0.3) + ggplot2::geom_pointrange(data = lizard_summary, ggplot2::aes(x = temperature, y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se, colour = population), position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.4)) + ggplot2::geom_line(data = lizard_summary, ggplot2::aes(x = temperature, y = mean, colour = population, group = population), position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.4)) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "#e12744")) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Test temperature (°C)", y = "Sprint speed (m/s)", colour = "Population") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week05_inference_files/figure-html/twoway-vis-1.png){width=624} ::: ::: The lines cross: coastal lizards are fastest at 28 °C, while inland lizards keep getting faster up to 36 °C. This suggests an interaction. ## 3. Check assumptions {.unnumbered} The assumptions are the same as for the one-way ANOVA. Fit the model first, then check the residuals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Two-way ANOVA with interaction. temperature * population is shorthand for # temperature + population + temperature:population lizard_aov2 <- aov(sprint_speed ~ temperature * population, data = lizard_data) performance::check_model(lizard_aov2, check = c("homogeneity", "qq")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week05_inference_files/figure-html/twoway-check-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: Both plots look fine and every lizard was tested only once, so the assumptions are met. ::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"} ## When is a two-way ANOVA NOT appropriate? (click to expand) - **Very unequal sample sizes** among the combinations, or missing combinations: the order of terms then changes the results. Keep designs balanced where possible (see [Research Design](research_design.qmd)). - **A numeric predictor** (e.g. body mass) as well as a factor: use a linear model with both (Week 7). - **Repeated measures**, e.g. the *same* lizard raced at all three temperatures: observations from one lizard are not independent, so use a mixed-effects model with lizard as a random effect (Week 12). - **Counts or yes/no responses**: use generalised linear models (Weeks 8 and 11). ::: ## 4. Model {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ANOVA table for the two-way model summary(lizard_aov2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) temperature 2 5.670 2.8350 51.482 3.37e-14 *** population 1 0.000 0.0004 0.007 0.93222 temperature:population 2 0.680 0.3401 6.177 0.00348 ** Residuals 66 3.634 0.0551 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: Because the interaction is significant, the next step is to compare temperatures **within each population**. `TukeyHSD()` on the interaction term compares all 15 pairs of the six groups. You only need the rows where the population is the same on both sides, e.g. `28:coastal-20:coastal` (coastal lizards at 28 °C minus coastal lizards at 20 °C). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # All pairwise comparisons of the 6 temperature x population groups TukeyHSD(lizard_aov2, which = "temperature:population") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Tukey multiple comparisons of means 95% family-wise confidence level Fit: aov(formula = sprint_speed ~ temperature * population, data = lizard_data) $`temperature:population` diff lwr upr p adj 28:coastal-20:coastal 0.73916667 0.45797958 1.02035375 0.0000000 36:coastal-20:coastal 0.48000000 0.19881292 0.76118708 0.0000618 20:inland-20:coastal 0.02416667 -0.25702042 0.30535375 0.9998544 28:inland-20:coastal 0.49666667 0.21547958 0.77785375 0.0000322 36:inland-20:coastal 0.71250000 0.43131292 0.99368708 0.0000000 36:coastal-28:coastal -0.25916667 -0.54035375 0.02202042 0.0877563 20:inland-28:coastal -0.71500000 -0.99618708 -0.43381292 0.0000000 28:inland-28:coastal -0.24250000 -0.52368708 0.03868708 0.1299626 36:inland-28:coastal -0.02666667 -0.30785375 0.25452042 0.9997638 20:inland-36:coastal -0.45583333 -0.73702042 -0.17464625 0.0001561 28:inland-36:coastal 0.01666667 -0.26452042 0.29785375 0.9999768 36:inland-36:coastal 0.23250000 -0.04868708 0.51368708 0.1621037 28:inland-20:inland 0.47250000 0.19131292 0.75368708 0.0000825 36:inland-20:inland 0.68833333 0.40714625 0.96952042 0.0000000 36:inland-28:inland 0.21583333 -0.06535375 0.49702042 0.2283272 ``` ::: ::: ## 5. Interpret {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ::: Always read the **interaction row first**. If the interaction is significant, the main effects can be misleading on their own. Here the main effect of population is not significant, yet the populations clearly respond differently to temperature. **Results sentence**: > The effect of temperature on sprint speed depended on population (two-way ANOVA, > temperature × population: *F*~2,66~ = 6.18, *p* = 0.003; Fig. 3). Coastal > lizards were fastest at 28 °C and slowed down at 36 °C, whereas inland lizards > continued to increase their speed up to 36 °C. Averaged over populations, speed > increased with temperature (*F*~2,66~ = 51.48, *p* < 0.001), and there was no overall > difference between populations (*F*~1,66~ = 0.01, *p* = 0.932). This is consistent with > inland lizards having a higher thermal optimum. # Writing results {.unnumbered} Every results statement should include: - the **direction** of the effect (higher, lower, increase, decrease); - the **magnitude** (how big is the difference, ideally with a 95% CI); - the **statistical support** (test statistic, degrees of freedom, *p*-value); - a **figure** showing the raw data and the means; - any **assumptions or caveats**. For example: *"Seedlings in the drought treatment grew half as fast as the well-watered control seedlings (control = 3.0 ± 0.45 mm/day, drought = 1.5 ± 0.31 mm/day; t~53~ = 5.06, p < 0.001; Fig. 2)."* # Assessment {.unnumbered} Task to complete before the end of the workshop. It goes on the **y-axis** and on the **left** of the `~` in a formula. 2. **Predictor variable (x)**: the groups or treatment you think *cause* the change. It goes on the **x-axis** and on the **right** of the `~`. 3. **Unit of replication**: what one row of the data represents (one quadrat, one plot, one lizard). Each row should be an independent replicate. A quick way to find them is to fill in this sentence: *"Does* **[response]** *differ between/among* **[groups of the predictor]***?"* For the lizard example: *"Does* **sprint speed** *differ among* **test temperatures***?"* gives `sprint_speed ~ temperature`. Then check the type of each variable with `dplyr::glimpse()`. For these tests the response must be **numeric** (`` or ``) and the predictor must be **categorical** (convert it with `factor()`). ::: **Question 1. Invasive plants and native species (*t*-test).** An exotic grass has spread into part of a native grassland. Ecologists suspect the grass crowds out native plants. They placed 1 m^2^ quadrats in the **invaded** area and in a nearby **uninvaded** area and counted the number of native plant species in each quadrat. **Hypothesis**: native plant species richness differs between invaded and uninvaded areas. | Variable in `invaded.csv` | Role | Type | Description | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | `Native_count` | Response (y) | Numeric (count) | Number of native plant species in a 1 m^2^ quadrat | | `Group` | Predictor (x) | Categorical, 2 levels | Whether the quadrat was in the `Invaded` or `Uninvaded` area | Each row is **one quadrat**, so quadrats are the replicates. a. Name the response and predictor variables, and say what one row of the data represents. Write the null and alternative hypotheses using these variables. b. Convert `Group` to a factor. Visualise `Native_count` for each `Group` (boxplot with the raw points) and calculate the mean, SD and *n* of each group. c. Check the assumptions (independence, normality, equal variances) and say whether each one is met. d. Run a Welch's *t*-test with the formula `Native_count ~ Group` and write a results sentence (direction, size of the difference, *t*, df and *p*). **Question 2. Plant species richness along an altitude gradient (one-way ANOVA).** Temperature and growing-season length change with altitude, which may affect how many plant species can live in a place. Plots were surveyed at **low**, **mid** and **high** altitude on a mountain and the number of plant species in each plot was recorded. **Hypothesis**: plant species richness differs among altitudes. | Variable in `altitude.csv` | Role | Type | Description | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | `Richness` | Response (y) | Numeric | Number of plant species recorded in a plot (estimated, so it has decimals) | | `Altitude` | Predictor (x) | Categorical, 3 levels | Altitude band of the plot: `Low`, `Mid` or `High` | Each row is **one plot**, so plots are the replicates. a. Name the response and predictor variables, say what one row represents, and write the null and alternative hypotheses. b. Convert `Altitude` to a factor in the order Low, Mid, High (otherwise R puts them in alphabetical order: High, Low, Mid). c. Visualise `Richness` for each `Altitude` and calculate descriptive statistics. d. Fit a one-way ANOVA with the formula `Richness ~ Altitude` and check its assumptions. e.
